Paper_name: Self processing in relation to emotion and reward processing in depression
Summary: Depression is characterised by a heightened self-focus believed to be associated with differences in emotion and reward processing. Adults experiencing varying levels of depression (n = 144) completed self-report depression measures (PHQ-9, BDI-II). Self, emotion and reward processing were measured separately and in combination using three cognitive tasks: a simple associative learning task (shape-label matching, self/emotion/reward conditions), a self-esteem go/no-go task, and a social evaluation learning task. When self processing was measured independently of emotion and reward in the associative learning task, there was little association with depression. However, when self and emotion processing occurred in combination (go/no-go task), depression was associated with an increased positive other bias (b = 3.51, 95% CI: 1.24, 5.79); when the self was processed in relation to emotion and reward (social evaluation learning task), depression was associated with reduced positive self biases (b = 0.11, 95% CI: 0.05, 0.17).
Author: Catherine Hobbs, Jie Sui, David Kessler, Marcus R. Munafò, Katherine S. Button
Conclusion: Depression was associated with enhanced positive implicit associations with others and reduced positive learning about the self, culminating in reduced self-favouring biases. When self, emotion and reward processing occurred independently in a simple associative learning task, there was little evidence of an association with depression. Treatments targeting reduced positive self-biases may provide more sensitive targets for therapeutic intervention and potential biomarkers of treatment responses.
